text: Governance answers one question: who gets to change the platform, and how? Not every multi-department organization needs Domain Separation's walled-off data model — most of them have a governance problem, and this chapter is where a Technical Architect actually solves it, deliberately, instead of letting it happen by accident.

Chapter 2's Domain Separation lesson ended on a promise: the real alternative to walling departments off inside the data model is governing how they're allowed to change the shared platform they all sit on top of. That's a process and ownership decision — no sys_domain field, no permanent tax on every future script and report.

Centralized governance has one platform team review and release every change. One naming convention, one view of the integration inventory, far fewer duplicate integrations or conflicting customizations — but every department's request queues behind the same small team, and the platform gets slower exactly as demand for it grows. Federated governance lets departments release inside established guardrails without routing every change through central approval. Delivery speed is the real win. The real risk is drift: departments independently rebuilding integrations, inventing contradictory role-naming conventions, abandoning shared patterns — without something actively holding the line.

Federation only survives on real, maintained guardrails: naming conventions consistent enough that two departments' tables and roles still read as one instance; mandatory code review, so autonomy to release never becomes autonomy to skip review; and a shared component library, so similar capabilities get built once and reused, not reinvented department by department. None of these are set-and-forget — a Technical Architect actively maintains them, the same way the integration inventory from Chapter 4 only stays useful if someone keeps updating it. Skip the upkeep and federated governance isn't governance at all — it's just no governance, with extra departments attached.

Choosing a governance model is only half the job. Next, Lesson 26 covers the other half: sequencing a real multi-department rollout, and deciding exactly which customizations stay shared across every department and which ones genuinely need to be built department-specific.
